en: Vaj 1; folio 26r1–v4 (Cz 27.1–1):
Homage to Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.
In the park of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great community of monks consisting of twelve hundred and fifty monks,
the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe,
entered the great city of Śrāvastī for alms.
Then the Blessed One, having walked for alms in the great city of Śrāvastī and returned after his meal, washed his feet and sat down on the seat prepared for him;
he sat cross-legged, holding his body erect and establishing mindfulness before him.
Then a great many monks approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and sat down to one side.
Now at that time, the venerable Subhūti was present and seated among that very assembly.

Then the venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
It is wonderful, Blessed One, how the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, has sustained the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, with the highest favor;
how the Tathāgata has entrusted the Bodhisattvas with the supreme entrustment.
How, Blessed One, should one who has set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle abide?
"How should one practice?
How should the mind be grasped?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is so, Subhūti. Bodhisattvas have been sustained by the Tathāgata with the supreme favor; bodhisattvas have been entrusted by the Tathāgata with the supreme entrustment.
Therefore, Subhūti, listen and attend well and properly; I shall speak."
How one who has set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle should stand, how they should practice, and how they should restrain their mind.
"So be it, Blessed One," the venerable Subhūti replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to them:
In this regard, Subhūti, those who have set out upon the Bodhisattva vehicle should generate the following thought:
"As many beings as are included in the enumeration of beings—whether born from eggs, or born from a womb, or born from moisture, or born spontaneously;
whether possessing form or formless; whether percipient, or non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—as far as they extend..."
As long as the realm of sentient beings is being conceptually designated, all of them must be led by me to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
In this way, though immeasurable sentient beings are to be led to final nirvana, not a single sentient being has been led to final nirvana.
Why is that?
If, Subhūti, the notion of a "being" arises for a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva.
Why is that?
Subhūti, he for whom the notion of a "being," or the notion of a "living soul," or the notion of a "person" arises, should not be called a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should not give a gift while established in anything;
he should give a gift without being established anywhere at all.
One should not give a gift while established in form; one should not give a gift while established in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give a gift:
such that he does not abide in the perception of signs.
For what reason?
Subhūti, it is not easy to grasp the measure of the mass of merit belonging to that bodhisattva who gives a gift without abiding anywhere.
What do you think, Subhūti? Is it easy to grasp the measure of space in the eastern direction?
Subhūti said,
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
It is likewise in the south, west, north, below, above, in the intermediate directions, and in the non-intermediate directions."
"In the ten directions, it is easy to grasp the measure of space. Subhūti said:
"No indeed, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"So it is, Subhūti."
"So it is, Subhūti. It is not easy to grasp the measure of the mass of merit of a bodhisattva who gives a gift without being established [in anything].
Nevertheless, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give a gift as this basis of meritorious action consisting of giving.
*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, folio 29r5–v4 (Cz 30.6–14).
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the Tathāgata to be seen by way of the perfection of his physical marks?
The Blessed One said: "The Tathāgata is not to be seen by way of the perfection of his physical marks. Why is that?"
"That perfection of marks which was described by the Tathāgata is itself a lack of perfection of marks.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, to whatever extent there is a mark, to that extent it is false."
To the extent that it is without characteristics, to that extent it is not false;
for in this way, by way of both having characteristics and being without characteristics, the Tathāgata is to be seen.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, will there be any beings in the future time, during the final five hundred years, who, when these very words of such sūtras are being spoken, [will have faith]?"
"They will produce the perception of a real entity.
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, do not speak thus."

There will be some beings who, in a future time, when such passages from these sūtras are being spoken, will conceive the notion that they are real. Moreover, Subhūti, in a future time, during the final five hundred years when the true Dharma is in decline, there will be bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who will be virtuous, endowed with qualities, and possessed of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti, these bodhisattvas will not have attended upon a single buddha,
nor will they have planted roots of merit under a single buddha.
Rather, Subhūti, they will have attended upon many buddhas and will have planted roots of merit under many buddhas.

Subhūti, those who, when such words of these sūtras are being spoken, shall obtain even a single moment of serene faith in their minds—they are known by the Tathāgata; they are seen by the Tathāgata. All of them will produce and take hold of an immeasurable mass of merit.
Why is that?
For indeed, Subhūti, in those bodhisattvas, the notion of a self will not arise; the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a soul, and the notion of a person will not arise.
Furthermore, Subhūti, in those bodhisattvas, the notion of a phenomenon will not arise, nor the notion of a non-phenomenon; neither a notion nor a non-notion will arise in them.
Why is that?
Subhūti, if the notion of a phenomenon (*dharmasaṃjñā*) should arise in those bodhisattvas, that itself would constitute for them a grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*),
a grasping at a being (*sattvagrāha*), a grasping at a soul (*jīvagrāha*), and a grasping at a person (*pudgalagrāha*).
If the notion of a non-phenomenon (*adharmasaṃjñā*) should arise, that too would constitute for them a grasping at a self.
"The apprehension of a being, the apprehension of a soul, and the apprehension of a person.
For what reason?
Indeed, Subhūti, neither dharma nor non-dharma should be grasped.
Therefore, with this in mind, the Tathāgata has spoken thus: "By those who understand the discourse on Dharma as being like a raft, even dharmas must be abandoned, let alone non-dharmas.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: Vaj 7; folio 31v6–32v1 (Cz 32.6–33.2).
What do you think, Subhūti? Is there any unexcelled, perfect enlightenment that has been fully realized by the Tathāgata? Or is there any dharma that has been taught by the Tathāgata?
Subhūti said:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, O Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as 'unexcelled perfect enlightenment,' nor is there any dharma whatsoever that has been taught by the Tathāgata."
For what reason? That Dharma which was taught by the Tathāgata is ungraspable and inexpressible.
That is neither dharma nor adharma. For what reason?
Because noble persons (āryapudgala) are characterized by the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
"What do you think, Subhūti? If someone were to fill this trichiliocosm, this great trichiliocosm of worlds, with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift—
what do you think, Subhūti, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?"
Subhūti said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
That son of good family or daughter of good family would, on that account, produce much merit."
For what reason?
Because that very thing, Blessed One, is not a heap.
Therefore the Tathāgata says, "A heap of merit is a non-heap," as the Blessed One has said.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill this trichiliocosm, the great trichiliocosm, with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift,
and if another were to take up even a single four-line verse from this Dharma-discourse and teach and elucidate it to others, the latter would on that account generate much more merit—
immeasurable and incalculable.
For what reason? Because, Subhūti, from this the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgatas is born;
and from this the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are born.
For what reason? Subhūti, as for these so-called "Buddha-dharmas," they are indeed not Buddha-dharmas at all.
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Does it occur to a stream-enterer, 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"For what reason?"
For he, Blessed One, has not entered into anything;
therefore he is called a "stream-enterer.
He has not entered into form, nor sounds, nor odors, nor tastes, nor tangibles, nor mental phenomena.
Therefore, he is called a "stream-enterer. The Blessed One said: [Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā 9b; folio 34v1–35r1 (Cz 34.12–18)] The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would it occur to a once-returner, 'I have attained the fruit of a once-returner'?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"For what reason?
It does not occur to a once-returner: 'I have attained the fruit of once-returning.'"
For what reason?
Because there is no such dharma that has attained the state of a once-returner;
therefore, he is called a "once-returner."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does it occur to a non-returner, 'I have attained the fruit of non-returning'?"
For what reason?
Because he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is called a "non-returner."
Therefore he is called a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
The Blessed One said: [Vajracchedikā 9d; folio 35r4–v2 (Cz 34.26–35.6)]
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does it occur to an Arhat, 'I have attained Arhatship'?
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
And why is that?
Because, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that is called 'Arhat'."
If, Blessed One, an Arhat were to think, "Arhatship has been attained by me," that itself would be for him a grasping at a self,
a grasping at a sentient being, a grasping at a living soul, and a grasping at a person.
“I am, Blessed One.”
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has declared me the foremost among those who dwell in the state of passionlessness. "Lord, I am an Arhat free from passion;
yet, Lord, it does not occur to me that 'I am an Arhat.'"
If, Blessed One, it should occur to me, "I have attained arhatship," the Tathāgata would not have prophesied of me,
"Subhūti is the foremost among those who dwell in non-contention."
The son of good family does not dwell anywhere;
therefore he is called "one who dwells in non-affliction," "one who dwells in non-affliction."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Has any dharma whatsoever been received by the Tathāgata from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
Subhūti replied,
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "There is no dharma whatsoever that was received by the Tathāgata from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, if any bodhisattva were to say, 'I shall bring about the array of buddha-fields,' he would be speaking falsely. Why is that?"
"Array of fields, array of fields," Subhūti—these have been spoken of by the Tathāgata as non-arrays. Therefore they are called "arrays of fields.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should generate a mind that is thus unestablished:
a mind should not be generated established in form;
a mind should not be generated established in sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental phenomena.
One should generate a mind that is not established anywhere.
Subhūti, it is as if there were a man whose physical body was like this: just like Sumeru, the king of mountains.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would that physical form be great? Subhūti said, "It would be great, Blessed One; it would be great, Sugata."
That would be his very self,
Blessed One. For what reason?
That which was spoken of by the Tathāgata as "self-existence" (ātmabhāva) is actually non-existence; therefore it is called "self-existence," for it is not an existent thing.
Therefore, it is called "personal existence" (ātmabhāva).
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, would they be many?"
"Would there then be many grains of sand in them?
Subhūti replied,
"Blessed One, those Ganges rivers alone would already be many, let alone the grains of sand within them."
The Blessed One said:

"I announce to you, Subhūti, I declare to you: suppose there were as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in all those rivers of the Ganges; and suppose some woman or man were to fill them with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Would that woman or man produce much merit on that account?
Subhūti said:
"Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata!
That woman or man would generate much merit on that account.
The Blessed One said:
Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone were to fill as many world-systems as those with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift,
and if another were to take up even a single four-line verse from this Dharma-discourse and teach it to others,
the latter would generate far more merit— immeasurable and incalculable— than the former.
Moreover, Subhūti, whatever spot of earth this Dharma-discourse is spoken or taught in, even if only a single four-line stanza from it, that spot of earth shall become a true shrine.
What need is there to speak, Subhūti, of those who will uphold this Dharma-discourse from among the world with its gods, humans, and asuras? They will be endowed with the highest marvel.
And in that region of earth, the Teacher dwells, or one or another who occupies the position of a teacher.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma-discourse, and how should I remember it?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
Subhūti, this Dharma discourse is named "The Perfection of Wisdom";
you should remember it thus.
And why is that?
Subhūti, that very perfection of wisdom which has been taught by the Tathāgata is itself a non-perfection.
"What do you think, Subhūti, is there any dharma whatsoever that has been taught by the Tathāgata?
Subhūti replied,
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
“Blessed One, there is no such dharma whatsoever that has been taught by the Tathāgata.
“Subhūti, as much as the dust of the earth in a great trichiliocosm world-system, would that be much?”
Subhūti said:
"It would be much, Blessed One; that particle of dust, Blessed One, would be great."
The "dust of the earth" spoken of by the Tathāgata has been spoken of by the Tathāgata as dustless;
that which is called "the dust of the earth" is what the Tathāgata has spoken of as a non-element (adhātu) when it is a world-system (lokadhātu).
That is called the world-system.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, to be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?"
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One. And why is that?"

“Those thirty-two marks of a great man, O Blessed One, which were spoken of by the Tathāgata were spoken of by the Tathāgata as being without marks; therefore they are called the ‘thirty-two marks of a great man. The Blessed One said: *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, 13e; folio 39v4–40r1 (Cz 39.1–8; G 5a3–5; P 182.20–183.3).
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a woman or a man were to relinquish as many bodily existences as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā,
and if another were to take up even a single four-line verse from this Dharma-discourse and teach it to others,
the latter would on that account generate far more merit— immeasurable and incalculable.
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti, through the force of the Dharma, shed tears. As he was shedding them, having wiped away his tears, he said this to the Blessed One:
It is marvelous, Blessed One!
It is most marvelous, Sugata,
that this Dharma-discourse has been spoken by the Tathāgata.
Since, Blessed One, knowledge has arisen in me, I have never before heard such a discourse on the Dharma;
it is supreme, Blessed One!
They will be endowed with wonder who, while this sutra is being spoken, will produce the perception of reality.
And that which, O Blessed One, is the perception of reality is itself a non-perception; therefore the Tathāgata says, "the perception of reality, the perception of reality."
"O Blessed One, it is not surprising to me that I should understand and have faith in this Dharma-discourse as it is being spoken.
But, O Blessed One, those who shall take up, master, and uphold this Dharma-discourse [are truly marvelous]."
They will be endowed with the most supreme wonders.
Furthermore, Blessed One, the notion of a self will not arise in them,
nor the notion of a sentient being, nor the notion of a living soul.
The notion of a person will not arise.
Why is that? Because that which is the notion of a self is itself a non-notion;
that which is the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a living soul, or the notion of a person is itself a non-notion.
For what reason?
Because the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are indeed free from all conceptualizations.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is! Those beings will be endowed with the most supreme wonder."
Those who, having heard this being spoken in this sutra, shall not tremble, shall not be terrified, and shall not fall into a state of terror— [they shall attain supreme enlightenment].
For what reason?
Subhūti, this has been taught by the Tathāgata as the supreme perfection;
and that supreme perfection which the Tathāgata teaches is taught by immeasurable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Therefore it is called the supreme perfection (*paramapāramitā*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is the Tathāgata’s perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) is itself a non-perfection (*apāramitā*).
For what reason?
Subhūti, when King Kaliṅga cut off my limbs and members, at that time I had no perception of a self, nor a perception of a sentient being, nor a perception of a soul, nor a perception of a person;
I had neither any perception nor any non-perception.
For what reason?
Subhūti, if at that time I had possessed the notion of a self,
I would also have possessed the notion of malice at that time.
"I recall, Subhūti, that in the past, during five hundred lifetimes, when I was a seer who preached forbearance, even then I had no perception of a self;
I had no perception of a sentient being, no perception of a living soul, and no perception of a person.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having abandoned all perceptions, should resolve their mind upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
One should not generate a mind that is established in form;
one should not generate a mind that is established in sound, odor, taste, or tangible objects;
one should not generate a mind that is established in mental phenomena.
One should not give rise to a mind established in non-dharma;
one should not give rise to a mind established anywhere.
For what reason?
That which is established is itself unestablished.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says: "One should give a gift without being established in form.
Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice the relinquishment of gifts for the sake of all sentient beings in this way:
whatever is the notion of a "sentient being" is itself a non-notion; those who are called "all sentient beings" by the Tathāgata are themselves non-beings.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata speaks what has come to be; the Tathāgata speaks the truth; the Tathāgata speaks according to reality; the Tathāgata does not speak falsely.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as for that dharma which has been fully awakened to or taught by the Tathāgata, therein there is neither truth nor falsehood.
Subhūti, it is just as if a man had entered into darkness;
in this way should a bodhisattva be regarded who, having fallen into a [conceptual] basis, relinquishes a gift that has fallen into a basis.
Subhūti, it is just as if a man with sight were to see various kinds of forms when the night has brightened and the sun has risen.
In this way, a bodhisattva is to be regarded who relinquishes a gift that has not fallen into [the category of] a thing.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who shall take up this Dharma-discourse...
They will uphold it,
they will recite it,
and they will master it.
Subhūti, those beings are known by the Tathāgata; Subhūti, they are seen by the Tathāgata; they are awakened to by the Tathāgata.
All those beings will produce an immeasurable mass of merit.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a woman or a man were to sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā during the morning time; if they were to sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā during the midday time and the evening time;
and if, in this manner, they were to sacrifice bodies for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons—
And whoever, having heard this Dharma-discourse,
does not reject it, would on that account produce a much greater mass of merit—
immeasurable and incalculable.
What need is there to mention one who, having written it down, would take it up, retain it, or recite it?
He should master it and reveal it in detail to others.
Moreover, Subhūti, this Dharma discourse is inconceivable and incomparable.
And this Dharma discourse has been taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of those beings who have set out upon the supreme vehicle,
and for the sake of those beings who have set out upon the most excellent vehicle.
Those who shall take up this Dharma-discourse, uphold it, and recite it.
Subhūti, those who master [this] will be known by the Tathāgata; Subhūti, they will be seen by the Tathāgata.
All those beings will be endowed with an immeasurable mass of merit.
They will be endowed with a mass of merit that is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and infinite.
Why is that?
Subhūti, it is not possible for those of inferior inclination to hear this Dharma.

It is not possible for those who hold the view of a self, nor those who hold the view of a sentient being, nor those who hold the view of a living soul, nor those who hold the view of a person, to hear, take up, retain, recite, or master this;
such a thing is impossible.
(Vajracchedikā 15c; folio 45r4-v2; Cz 44.13-18; G 7a2-3; P 186.17-20)
Moreover, Subhūti, whichever spot of earth this sutra shall be proclaimed,
that spot of earth will become worthy of worship;
that spot of earth will become worthy of being saluted and circumambulated by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
And that spot of earth shall become a *caitya*. Subhūti, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who shall take up, retain, and master such discourses as these— Vaj 16a;
P 186.20–187.3) [as above]... Subhūti, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who shall take up, retain, and master such discourses as these—
They will be despised, and they will be thoroughly despised.
Whatever past-life karmas those beings have committed that would lead to the lower realms, they will exhaust those unwholesome karmas from previous lives through being humiliated in this very life,
and they shall attain the awakening of a Buddha.

I recall, Subhūti, in a past time, more than incalculable aeons ago, even further back than that, there were eighty-four hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, beginning with Dīpaṃkara, whom I propitiated; having propitiated them, I did not fail them.

And, Subhūti, that which I have pleased the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, having pleased them I did not displease them; and that which they shall take up, uphold, recite, and master this sūtra in the final period, during the last five hundred years— [these two are equal].
Subhūti, compared to this mass of merit, that previous mass of merit does not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part,
nor a hundred-thousandth part,
nor even a hundred-thousand-millionth part.
It does not admit of being reckoned by number, nor by part, nor by calculation, nor by comparison, nor by analogy. Subhūti,
if one were to speak of the mass of merit of those sons of good family or daughters of good family, [it would be impossible to describe].
Whatever mass of merit those sons of good family or daughters of good family may acquire at that time,
those beings would fall into madness or undergo distraction of mind.
[The manuscript breaks off here.]
